units.en: unlike with the microsoft compiler gcc still allows you to create inline assembly even for 64-bit code microsoft used to allow that for 32-bit but then they deprecated it and disallowed it in 64-bit code so when you're writing in-line assembly for gcc you're going to use the canoe assembler or gas syntax and it's going to expect things to be written in at t syntax the general form is that you will have the keyword asm parentheses quotes and then some number of instructions separated by a explicit

slash n new line close print uh close quotes close parentheses semicolon so you could have a single instruction like this asm no op and then semicolon it's done sm move one two three four to eax and then it's done but if you don't want to keep writing the asm over and over again instead you would write asm once you'd have quotes and then you would have however many assembly instructions you want with an explicit slash n between the assembly instructions so here we can see something that's six instructions long

now i highly recommend that you take a look at this gas syntax tutorial because it's extremely helpful for letting you get much more deep than i'm going to go into one of the important things that is talked about in that how-to guide is extended asm syntax in this form you can have the assembly template separated by a colon from output operands input operands and a list of clobbered registers meaning things that this assembly is guaranteed to be overwriting it's basically a hint

to the compiler saying hey just so you know this assembly sequence is going to destroy the value in this register so you should you know perhaps save it before you get in here or restore it afterwards now each of these things output operands input operands and cloud registers is optional so it's not actually required but when you're using extended asm you would still need to have these colons and you just put nothing in between them so down here let's look at an example we have a

single local variable myvar which is an int set to abcd and if the assembly wanted to make use of that myvar value then they could for instance have a move long and this percent 0 is basically going to be something that's interpolated or filled in with some other value and the value that it's going to be filled in with is the myvar so move percent 0 comma and then now it starts using double percents percent percent so that it's kind of differentiating a single percent is used for interpolation of some input or

output operand and double percent signs are then used for just saying you know specifically some register so it's moving percent 0 which is going to be my var that is going to be an input operand so we can see that we've got the assembly template here then there's a colon and there's nothing written here so that would be the output operands there's no output operands and then a colon and the input operands so input operands is this quote r for register and then parenthesis my var to

say it's basically pulling my var into you know this location right here so this would be reading in my var into the ax register then you could have some other assembly that just covers the value with one two three four into eax and then if you wrote that as output you would have move al eax which was now one two three four and that would be written into percent zero which will be the zero with output operand so you can see here we have the colon and then output operands this is
